title: Wesley Sews Up First Titled Tuesday Of 2026
summary: GM Wesley So won Titled Tuesday on September 29, starting 7/7 on his way to a 9.5-point total. That score was enough for an outright victory after the top three boards in the final round, including his own, all ended in draws. One of the key figures of the upcoming Grandmasters documentary, So scored his first Titled Tuesday victory of the year, and fifth in just 75 attempts ever (a 6.7% win rate better than most 10-time winners). GM Denis Lazavik took second place with the top tiebreak in a seven-way tie on nine points. In case you missed it, here's this week's broadcast with GM Robert Hess: https://t.co/tRvPHraUOjThe Olympiad proved to be a useful warm up after all for the real event! @chesscom 😀🏆 🥇 🎉💪 So and Lazavik were among the 17 players to start 4/4, a list that did not include some usual suspects such as GM Hikaru Nakamura, who reached a Chess.com record 3470 blitz rating just before the event started, or last week's victor GM Alireza Firouzja, whose third-round win over GM Luca Moroni led Hess to the line of the week when he spotted the position after 21 moves: "I've never been more confused ever looking at a chess game... Can I resign for both players?" In the wild position, Moroni went for broke, but there was no mate to be found as Firouzja picked up a second queen and the win.

title: Dream Olympiad For Uzbekistan: 13 Samarkand 2026 Conclusions
summary: Uzbekistan's victory in the Chennai Olympiad of 2022 was sweet, but regaining the title on home soil in the 46th Chess Olympiad 2026 is even sweeter. title: Texas Tech Defeats 3-Time Champion Mizzou As Fall CCL Season Begins
summary: The Collegiate Chess League, the leading online chess competition for college students, started with two tight matches and one blowout in the top division's opening round. Texas Tech defeated three-time league champions the University of Missouri (Mizzou) 9-7. The University of Texas at Dallas (UTD) began their title defense by narrowly winning a finals rematch with SRM Institute of Science and Technology, 8.5-7.5. Saint Louis University (SLU) dominated their match against The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, 15-1. CCL Division 1 Standings Mizzou is a perennial CCL powerhouse, having made the finals five times this decade. title: WSTC 2026 European Stage begins in Tsaghkadzor
summary: The European Continental Stage of the FIDE ISCF World Schools Team Championship 2026 commenced on 29 September in Tsaghkadzor, Armenia. 27 school teams from 25 nations are competing in the final qualifying stage for places in the Grand Final in December. The stage is organised by the International School Chess Federation (ISCF) together with FIDE, the Chess Federation of Armenia, and Freedom Corp. as sponsor. Tournament format Each team fields four players and one reserve, boys and girls. The tournament is an eight-round Swiss, played under time control of  45 minutes plus a 10-second increment per move from move one. Riga State Gymnasium No.1 (average rating 1989) tops the starting rankings, followed by Gymnasium No.50 of Minsk, Belarus and Tallinna Tonismae Reaalkool, Estonia. Armenia is represented by 3 schools, led by Yerevan’s basic school N 77. Opening ceremony: Peru sends the message The ceremony opened with a film about the championship and its journey so far, through the stages already held in Asia, Africa and the Americas. The first to welcome the players was Grandmaster Smbat Lputian, founder of the Chess Academy of Armenia and Vice President of the Chess Federation of Armenia. Then, as has become a tradition at every stage of the championship, the floor passed to the children from the previous stage. This time the message came from the winners themselves. On screen, the players of Saco Oliveros de Lince, champions of the American Continental Stage in San José, greeted the teams gathered in Tsaghkadzor. They had also sent postal cards, each carrying one message about chess, and the officials came on stage to read them out, letting the Peruvian players’ words stand in for their own. Breaking stereotypes“Don’t be afraid to make an unusual move, even if no one has played it before. Sometimes the most unexpected move changes the whole game!” said Nadzeya Krauchuk, Tournament Director of the FIDE ISCF World Schools Team Championship Love chess, no matter what“Sometimes we lose, sometimes we make mistakes, and sometimes we feel like flipping the board! But every game teaches us something new. A true love of the game does not end with a defeat!” said Ion-Serban Dobronauteanu, Director of Youth Chess of the European Chess Union. Chess opens the door to friendship“We may speak different languages and live on different continents. But once we sit down at the same chessboard, we understand each other,” said Varduhi Sargsyan, Executive Director of the Chess Academy of Armenia. You don’t have to be a champion to enjoy the game“Not all of us have a champion’s trophy at home. But everyone can enjoy a beautiful game, a clever move, or a small personal victory,” said Timur Turlov, President of FIDE and President of ISCF. This continues a tradition that runs through the championship: in San José, the ceremony opened with gifts sent by players from the African stage. This time the message came from the Americas and was addressed to Europe. For Timur Turlov, President of FIDE and President of ISCF, it was the first tournament opening since his election as FIDE President at the 46th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand. He thanked the Armenian hosts and called Armenia “one of the world’s great chess centers and the home of many outstanding players.” He pointed to Armenia’s own example. In 2011 it became the first country to make chess a compulsory subject in primary schools, and fifteen years later many countries are learning from that experience. Demand for school chess is growing worldwide, he said, and delegates from many countries raised it with him in Samarkand. It will be one of FIDE’s main priorities during his presidency. Timur Turlov then announced FIDE’s plans to allocate $1,000,000 a year to chess in education worldwide under the new FIDE Development Fund. The money will help national federations train teachers and give schools teaching materials and equipment. “Our goal is to give many more children the opportunity to discover chess at school,” he said. He ended with a word to the players: “Play boldly, respect your opponents, and support your teammates. I wish you great games, new friendships, and unforgettable days in Armenia.” Then he declared the European stage of the World School Team Championship open and made the first ceremonial move to start the competition.  Round 1 Four matches ended with 4-0 clean sweeps: Gymnasium No. 50 of Minsk – British School of Kosova;Green Village School – Naum Naumovski Borche;ZS Wolkerova Bardejov – Privates Gymnasium Sacre Coeur Wien;Tasen skole – Vesturbaejarskoli. The top-seeded Latvian team opened the European Continental Stage with a convincing 3-1 victory over Armenia’s “Mkhitar Sebastatsi” Educational Complex. Round 2 In Round 2, Riga State Gymnasium No. 1 secured a 3½-½ victory, while Gymnasium No. 50 of Minsk won 4-0 again, and Tallinna Tõnismäe Reaalkool claimed a 3-1 win. After two rounds as many as five teams are on 4/4 match points, with Gymnasium No. 50 of Minsk leading with the perfect 8/8 game points.  Beyond the board After two rounds of chess, players took part in an Armenian Carpet Weaving Workshop, an introduction to one of the country’s oldest crafts. Armenian carpets have been woven by hand for centuries, knot by knot, with patterns and symbols passed down from one generation to the next. For players who had spent the day thinking in squares and diagonals, the workshoo offered a different kind of grid, one built slowly by hand, one knot at a time. The day ended with the movie “Time from,” a quieter close to a long first day before Round 3. Official website: https://worldschoolteam2026.fide.com/

title: Bodhana Sivanandan: Youngest-Ever WGM at 11
summary:
The English Chess Federation put its youngest player on top board for the Women's Olympiad in Samarkand: Bodhana Sivanandan, just 11 years old. This did not come as a complete surprise, as with her rating of 2354 (before the Olympiad), she was and remains England's number one female player, some way ahead of the experienced Jovanka Houska and Harriet Hunt, both of whom, however, are already somewhat past their peak.

Bodhana Siv anand an ( Notice anything? Surely that can't be a coincidence. And here too: Praggn anand haa.) repaid the faith placed in her with her performance. The 11-year-old played all eleven rounds and scored eight points on top board. After three wins, she drew against the strong Azerbaijani player Ulviyya Fataliyeva in round four and, for example, also held the world's top junior and reigning European Women's Champion Anastasiia Hnatyshyn to a draw. The experienced Nana Dzagnidze was also unable to get the better of Bodhana Sivanandan. The English player suffered just one defeat, in round eight against Peru's Deysi Cori.

With her performance, Bodhana Sivanandan finished 13th in the list of the best players on board one. She was the best player on her team and led England to 15th place in the final standings, five places higher than their starting rank based on average rating.

The result also earned her a WGM norm (Woman Grandmaster). It was Bodhana's third norm, meaning she has now fulfilled the requirements for the title. She is thus the youngest WGM in chess history, succeeding Kateryna Lagno, who received the title in 2002 at the age of twelve. Hou Yifan, later Women's World Champion, also received the title at the age of 12, in 2007. FIDE introduced the WGM title in 1976.

Bodhana's interest in chess began when a visitor to her parents' home left behind a chessboard at the start of the pandemic. Her father taught her the rules, and she improved her game with the help of YouTube tutorials. In 2021, she played her first tournament at the Harrow Chess Club. In 2022, at the age of seven, Bodhana won all 24 of her games at the European Schools Chess Championship. In the summer of 2026, she became the youngest British national champion of all time.

title: Interview with the Olympic winners from Uzbekistan: "We have many more victories to come!"
summary:
Nobody came close!

The Uzbekistan Open team has done it again! After stunning the chess world by winning the Olympiad in 2022, they are champions once again, this time on home soil at the 46 th FIDE Chess Olympiad!

Uzbekistan took gold with 20 match points and 32½ game points | Source: ChessBase Olympiad portal

We caught up with the gold medal-winning team after the closing ceremony to relive the key moments, the pressure of playing at home, and the team spirit behind the title.

Interview by Sagar Shah

Sagar Shah: Congratulations, guys, you have won the gold! In 2022, we had an interview. Four years later, you guys are champions again, this time in Uzbekistan. How are you feeling?

Sindarov: We feel fantastic. Very happy to win the Olympic gold medal in our country. We are very proud to become champions in our home country, where everyone supports us.

Raw moments from Samarkand as Uzbekistan wins the Chess Olympiad 2026 | Video: ChessBase India

Sagar: You have won a beautiful trophy. I want to start this interview with your game, Javokhir, the queen sacrifice (against Diego Saul Rodri from Peru). I think it was very beautiful: 31...Kf7 and then 32...Rh3. What a game!

Sindarov sacrificed his queen by playing 31...Kf7! Can you find the reason behind the move?

Sindarov: The game was interesting, but in the end, you know, it was just a choice. Any other move was around nine or ten moves long, but 31...Kf7 was just making some aura. I was thinking during the game that maybe I shouldn't play this move, but in the end I decided, okay, come on, let's play for some videos, for some content, real stuff. But it's an easy move. I won't say it's something crazy.

Sagar: Nodirbek, you have two gold medals. You were incredible on board one, like a machine. You didn't lose a game. You won game after game. Brilliant play!

Nodirbek played all the rounds and didn't lose a single game! | Source: Chess results

Nodirbek: I am extremely happy to be part of this incredible team. These guys are simply the best on their boards, and in chess in general. They all belong in the top ten. They play at a very high level. I am lucky to have such strong teammates, and I am proud to be here with the boys, with everyone. I did my job on the first board. I played very safe at times and won some games as well. I worked very hard before this tournament, so I wouldn't let the team down, and I am very happy that I succeeded.

Not a single loss he faced! | Photo: Michal Walusza

Sagar: Yakubboev, you were the guy who won so many critical games. Against Türkiye, you scored the win. Against India, you scored the win again.

Yakubboev: This time I had this role, let's say: winning important games. But the other teammates also performed very well. It wasn't planned. It wasn't a planned situation. Somehow I finished last, and I somehow managed to win. But I am happy to get a point for our team. This time I had this role. (Smiles)

Yakubboev in demand! | Photo: Michal Walusza

Sagar: Tell us about your game with Nihal, this 39...Nxh4, this 39.gxh4+ Nxh4. What a moment that was. Maybe the most important moment of the Olympiad, would you say?

A terrible blunder by Nihal, 37...Nf5? , which made him lose his queen. Can you find out how?

Yakubboev: I think so, because the match against India was the most important for us. It decided the whole standings. After that match, we could really fight for a medal. If we had lost that match, I don't think we would have tried to win this medal. It was important. And he missed that 38.Ne6+ check. I saw it earlier, when he took on g5. I saw ...Kg7, which is a winning move. When he took on g5, I felt a bit happy. Then I played 37.g3 , and it was already a complicated game. I was not worse; I was in the game. ...Kg7 was the decisive moment for our team.

Nodirbek: He wasn't the only one who was happy after 36...Kg5 . We were all watching his game like crazy. We went crazy after 38...Ne6+. Our chat was screaming.

Sagar: Were you doing live commentary, or were you just watching privately?

Sindarov: On Lichess.

A crucial victory for Uzbekistan as they defeated India in round six | Photo: Michal Walusza

Sagar: Shamsiddin, you played 11...b5 against Gukesh in the opening. I think it was an incredible hold with the black pieces, and a very important game. You gave him no chance.

Shamsiddin: Yeah, I know the lines. It was preparation. I saw it one or two months ago, not on the preparation day. I just remembered it. I know that after b5 it's easy to equalise. We are all happy to have won. We won all the important matches: USA, India and China. We are all happy.

Sagar: Mukhiddin, I have to tell you, the last round you played so good. And you had another victory yesterday. That was just insane. How did you find those amazing moves like 29.d5 and 30.h5?

Mukhiddin: In general, I am very happy. I didn't feel a lot of pressure on this team, since I have a very strong team, as you can see. I just tried to play simple chess, and if I got a chance, I tried to use it. Yesterday, when I was playing against Gabriel Sargissian, I felt after the opening that my position was slightly better, so I started to push.

Black played 27...Qb7? . Can you find a better move?

At some point it was close to equal, but then he missed it and blundered with 27...Qb7 . I played 28.Bb5 . I felt that 28...Nd8 was very bad. I pushed 29.d5 , and after he took on d5, I played 30.h5 . I felt that his king was in trouble, so that's why I went for it.

Sagar: Amazing. Nodirbek, Javokhir spoke about this aura moment. I think you playing 1.e4 d5 was one such aura moment. There's a nice reel where you played it, everyone smiled, and then you smiled too.

Nodirbek: Yeah. I told them about twenty minutes before the game that I would play d5, and everyone went crazy. At first they didn't believe I would play it, and then when they saw...

Yakubboev: But we discussed it in the team meeting.

Nodirbek: Yeah, we discussed it briefly in the team meeting. I had some options, like ...c5, the Caro-Kann or the Scandinavian, but I said I would decide myself. In preparation, I saw that he has no practice at all in the Scandinavian, so I tried it against him, and it worked. The whole idea was inspired by Arjun, as I said. He played it in the last round in Budapest and won a nice game, so I also tried to steal his aura.

Sagar: And Javokhir, you played Nf3 and b3 (against Robert Hovhannisyan from Armenia) with such good preparation. I think you were prepared until around move 20.

Javokhir: Yeah, but because of that good preparation, it was just equal in the end. But my opponent somehow played a really bad game in this match. I got lucky. He started giving me his first and second pawns; I captured all of them, and I won a game I didn't expect to win. I was really shocked by how my opponent played. Robert is generally a very solid player, but in this game he somehow played really badly, which surprised me. But it was good preparation. Sometimes you need to be lucky to win this tournament.

Sagar: Today, against Ivanchuk, was also a tough game.

Javokir: Yeah, a very tough game.

Sagar: At one point you thought for 40 minutes and played 14...Na5.

Javokhir: Yeah, I was trying to remember the line because I had seen it somewhere before the tournament. I was checking that line because I had played some blitz games here. Then somehow I forgot it, and I tried to remember the best equalising move, but I couldn't. It was a very unhappy moment. I tried to remember for 40 minutes, but I didn't find it. I played a move of my own, and it really wasn't a good one. Then he got some advantage, but I managed to draw, which made the team happy, and we won. When I draw, I understand that we will win the match easily.

Prime Minister of Uzbekistan Abdulla Aripov visited the Chess Olympiad 2026 | Photo: Rafal Oleksiewicz

title: The dark side of the online world: Hannah Sayce's story
summary:
Hannah Sayce from Melbourne has had a remarkable career in chess. At the start of the pandemic, when she was 19, she began taking an interest in the game and played on the usual online platforms to pass the time. She started with a rating of 1000 and, in a relatively short period of time, reached an impressive online blitz rating of 2300 in tournaments on chess.com.

As she enjoyed chess so much, she eventually began playing classical over-the-board tournaments. The transition was difficult at first, as Hannah Sayce still had to learn that with a classical time control one has to think about decisions for longer, and that the endgame takes on greater importance.

Hannah Sayce travelled to open tournaments in Europe and Asia and began sharing her chess experiences through streams on Twitch. Before long, Hannah Sayce had tens of thousands of chess fans following her on that platform. Several companies support her chess activities.

Hannah Sayce | Photo: Private, via Facebook

Not all of her fans, however, responded in the way she would have wanted. In April 2024, one fan began harassing the young chess streamer. Shumsheer Singh Ghumman, a 47-year-old café owner, gathered information about Hannah Sayce and her family, obtained the contact details of her friends and threatened her. He claimed that he would use AI to find out further information and use it against her. He also found out about Hannah Sayce's holiday and travel plans. In March 2025, Hannah Sayce obtained a restraining order against the stalker, but this did not stop Shumsheer Singh Ghumman from continuing to harass her.

After Shumsheer Singh Ghumman learned that Hannah Sayce intended to travel to Qatar, he informed the local authorities and claimed that she would be smuggling drugs into the country hidden inside her chess pieces. Hannah Sayce was detained on arrival at the airport and temporarily held in prison until the matter could be cleared up.

The same thing happened when she tried to enter Iceland for the Reykjavík Open. Once again, the stalker had informed the local authorities and falsely accused his victim of drug smuggling. Once again, Hannah Sayce was arrested.

Eventually, the Australian authorities took decisive action against the stalker. On 1 May 2026, Shumsheer Singh Ghumman was arrested at his café in Burnley, in eastern Melbourne. On 23 May, the matter came before the court with a total of 35 charges. It emerged that Shumsheer Singh Ghumman had previously been convicted in a similar, but even more serious, case. He had set fire to the home of a woman whom he had also stalked and had been sentenced at the time to nine years in prison for attempted murder and arson. On appeal, the sentence was later reduced to four years.

At the opening of the proceedings, the judge rejected an application for bail because, in her view, Ghumman posed a threat to Hannah Sayce's safety. The hearing will continue in October. Until then, the stalker will remain in custody.

Hannah Sayce expressed surprise on her channels that the story had been published in the Australian media. She herself had not spoken to the media, which had apparently obtained the information from the court hearing. "Although I had not expected to speak about this publicly, I am honestly relieved to be able to get it off my chest. The last couple of years have been very difficult, and the wrongful detention in Qatar was, to put it mildly, a very frightening experience", she commented on the matter.

Last Sunday, the streamer was a guest at Judit Polgar's "Global Chess Festival" and took part in a clock simultaneous exhibition given by the Hungarian chess icon. She streamed the game live on her Twitch channel.

title: Clear win for China in Women's Chess Olympiad, while Kazakhstan and India complete the podium
summary:
Zhu Jiner excels across the board

The Chinese team remained unbeaten in the women's section. The team suffered only two individual losses in total. The Chinese women also won in round eleven, defeating Vietnam 3-1. In the team matches in which they suffered an individual defeat, China drew 2-2 instead of winning. With a total of 20 match points, China pulled clear of the competition and won gold. Zhu Jiner also stood out with her individual performance on board one. For scoring 7 points from 9 appearances and achieving a tournament performance rating of 2638, Zhu received individual gold. According to the live ratings, she gained 9 Elo points, bringing her to 2554 in the live ratings . This makes her the world number two among women again in the live ratings, behind Hou Yifan, who has a rating of 2596.

Several of Zhu Jiner's teammates also finished in the top ten on their respective boards. Like Zhu Jiner, Lu Miaoyi finished first in the individual standings on board three. She scored 9½ points from 11 games and achieved a tournament performance rating of 2576.

Frederik Svane and Lu Miaoyi win individual gold (board three) | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

For her results on board two, Song Yuxin received the bronze medal in the individual standings. She scored 8 points from 11 games and achieved a tournament performance rating of 2492. On the reserve board, Mo Zhai finished sixth in the individual standings with 5 points from 8 games and a tournament performance rating of 2295.

China team statistics

China defeats Vietnam 3-1

China secured first place on their own terms with a 3-1 victory over Vietnam. Kazakhstan were able to hold on to second place because they ultimately had one match point more than India and the USA, who would otherwise have had the better tiebreak.

China against Vietnam in round eleven | Photo: Rafal Oleksiewicz / FIDE

Lu Miaoyi 1–0 Phuong Hanh Luong

In the game between Lu Miaoyi and Phuong Hanh Luong, Lu Miaoyi gained a large advantage in the endgame after her opponent surely regretted considering the alternatives instead of playing a mistaken knight manoeuvre.

With this move, Black wins a pawn and attacks the bishop directly. White, however, wants to move the bishop to e7 anyway. After 41.Be7 , Rh6 to protect the pawn would have failed because 42.Re4+ wins the knight. Black therefore played 41...Ng6 , and 42.Bxd6 followed immediately. Had Black not captured the pawn beforehand and instead played 40...Ng3, e4 would have been protected and the rook could not have attacked the king via that square. Then 41.Be7 Kf4 could also have followed, and if the bishop subsequently captured on d6, the trap would spring with 42...Ne4+ (a double attack on the king and bishop). In addition, Rh6 becomes possible for Black after 40...Ng3 because e4 would be protected.

The game ended when White was three pawns up, including connected passed pawns.

Kazakhstan take silver

In round eleven, Poland and Kazakhstan drew, as did India and Georgia. The United States defeated Romania 3-1. Kazakhstan therefore kept the USA at a distance with their draw and were fortunate that India did not defeat Georgia.

Earlier, in round five, she had also drawn against Humpy Koneru (2509). Kiolbasa gained 19 Elo points from the tournament. Poland missed out on the team bronze medal by the narrowest of margins. Even so, the Polish team certainly need not reproach themselves for failing to defeat Kazakhstan.

The race for third place

The battle for third place was extremely close. Five teams finished the tournament with 17 match points: India, United States, Poland, Armenia and Mongolia. The tiebreak ultimately decided the matter in India's favour.

title: Uzbekistan triumph on home soil, collect second Olympiad gold
summary:
Uzbekistan, India and Germany on the podium

Uzbekistan completed their home Olympiad with gold after defeating Ukraine 2½–1½ in Sunday's final round in Samarkand. The hosts finished on 20/22 match points, two clear of India and Germany, to claim their second Olympiad title after their breakthrough victory in Chennai four years ago.

The decisive point against Ukraine came on board four, where Mukhiddin Madaminov defeated 18-year-old European champion Roman Dehtiarov. The other three games ended drawn: Nodirbek Abdusattorov shared the point with Igor Kovalenko, Javokhir Sindarov drew Vasyl Ivanchuk and Nodirbek Yakubboev was held by Ihor Samunenkov.

Uzbekistan therefore finished with ten match wins and a single defeat, against Germany in round eight. Their campaign was built not only on the results of their highest-rated players, but on a remarkably balanced lineup which repeatedly produced points on all four boards.

Time to celebrate! The Uzbek team headed by team captain (and 2004 FIDE World Championship winner) Rustam Kasimdzhanov | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

"This is the proudest moment in my life"

The title has a clear link with Uzbekistan's first Olympiad triumph in Chennai in 2022. Four members of this year's five-player squad - Abdusattorov, Yakubboev, Sindarov and Shamsiddin Vokhidov - were also part of that gold-medal team. The current squad is still exceptionally young. All five players are between 19 and 24 years old, with Yakubboev and Vokhidov the oldest members at 24.

Abdusattorov was again the leading figure. He played in all eleven rounds and finished unbeaten on 8½/11, taking individual gold on board one with a 2869 TPR. He had previously won individual silver on the top board at both the 2022 and 2024 Olympiads. Speaking to chess.com's Mike Klein, the Uzbek star noted :

This is the proudest moment in my life. It's been a tremendous achievement for our team, for Uzbekistan. I'm truly happy.

It was a dream tournament for Nodirbek Abdusattorov | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

There were individual medals further down the Uzbek lineup as well. Sindarov took bronze on board two, while Yakubboev collected silver on board three.

Four of the five Uzbek players also gained rating in Samarkand, with Vokhidov the lone exception. Abdusattorov gained 18.0 Elo points and Yakubboev 14.4. Sindarov and Abdusattorov now occupy 4 th and 5 th place respectively in the live world rankings, while Yakubboev has entered the 2700 club and sits 26 th on 2712.

Dehtiarov v. Madaminov

Madaminov converted this pawn-up rook endgame to get the crucial win for the local heroes. Dehtiarov here faltered with 33.b4? , when 33.Re5 was the only move that would have kept drawing chances for White (rook endgames often require extreme precision!).

The black king soon gained activity in the centre, and Madaminov continued to play precisely until simplifying into an endgame with rook against rook and pawn.

This is the position after 46...Kd4 . Madaminov correctly calculated that he can give up his pawn on f4 in order to capture the white lone solider on b4.

The rest was simple for the 19-year-old Uzbek grandmaster, who is likely to remember this endgame by heart for the rest of his life!

Uzbekistan facing Ukraine | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

India take silver despite Gukesh defeat

Given Uzbekistan's consistency, India's silver medal represented a strong result for the second seeds. Their final match against Hungary ended 2–2, although the result came in an unexpected fashion. Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu drew Richard Rapport and Nihal Sarin shared the point with Benjamin Gledura, while the remaining two games were decisive.

Gleb Dudin defeated Gukesh Dommaraju on board four, while Arjun Erigaisi beat Peter Leko to restore equality and secure the match point India needed for silver.

Gukesh had arrived at the final round with an exceptional 8½/10 score, but Dudin's win pushed him down to individual silver on board four. The result ended a sequence in which Gukesh had taken gold for his individual performances on board one at both Chennai 2022 -when he represented India 2 - and Budapest 2024.

The defeat cost Gukesh 6.9 rating points on the day, although he still gained 7.1 Elo points over the Olympiad as a whole. He leaves Samarkand ranked 29 th in the world and 72 points behind 2782-rated Sindarov, his opponent in the World Championship match that begins in Geneva in less than two months.

Praggnanandhaa also left Samarkand with an individual medal, taking bronze on board one with a 2772 performance rating.

Reigning world champion Gukesh Dommaraju | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

Dudin v. Gukesh

Gukesh's handling of a rather double-edged Sicilian was rather adventurous. By move 10, he had lost the right to castle, while by move 21 he was already a pawn down.

In the diagram above, Dudin had already consolidated his position, with the pair of knights a much stronger duo than the black bishop pair - after 26.c5 , the outpost on d6 becomes the key factor in the position.

Dudin patiently improved his position in the ensuing manoeuvring phase. By move 41, he was already two pawns up with a strong passer on d6.

Gukesh continued playing until move 59, but he would have probably resigned earlier had this not been a team event.

The golden generation of Indian chess won the 2024 Olympiad and now took silver in Samarkand | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

Germany return to the Olympiad podium

Germany took bronze after beating the Netherlands 2½–1½, finishing level with India on 18/22 but behind the defending champions on tiebreaks.

Matthias Bluebaum scored the decisive point by defeating Jorden van Foreest on board two, while Anish Giri drew Vincent Keymer, Loek van Wely drew Frederik Svane and Casper Schoppen shared the point with Rasmus Svane.

The medal ends a 26-year wait for Germany. Their previous team medal in the open section of a Chess Olympiad came in Istanbul 2000, when a team headed by Artur Yusupov and the late Robert Hübner took silver.

Germany's path to bronze featured nine match victories and two losses, without a single draw. Those defeats came against China and India, while they were the only team in the tournament to defeat eventual champions Uzbekistan.

Frederik Svane was their standout performer for a second Olympiad in a row. He played in all eleven rounds and finished undefeated on 8½/11, corresponding to a 2796 performance rating and individual gold on board three. It was his second successive individual Olympiad gold, after he had scored 8/9 on board five in Budapest two years ago.

Frederik Svane (right) took home individual gold in two consecutive editions of the Chess Olympiad! | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

Bluebaum v. Van Foreest

The game developed in Bluebaum's favour when Van Foreest had to give up the exchange in the endgame. The sequence began with an exchange in which the German grandmaster gave up two pieces for a rook.

The sequence would not have been a problem for Van Foreest had it not been followed by Bluebaum's key move: 29.Qa3! , with a double attack on the knight and bishop.

Black also picked up the a-pawn for the bishop, but the Dutchman could no longer save the game. The encounter ended after 64 moves in a pawn ending that was lost for Black.

Matthias Bluebaum was Germany's hero in round eleven | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

Germany reached the podium in the Olympiad for the first time in 26 years! | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

Four teams on 17/22, including United States

Four teams ended a match point behind India and Germany on 17/22: the United States, Azerbaijan, Armenia and Hungary. The Americans took fourth place on tiebreaks.

For the top-seeded United States, fourth place will inevitably look less impressive than their starting position suggested. They were never quite able to rejoin the fight for first place after losing to Germany in round five and drawing Armenia in round seven. They nevertheless finished with a clear 3–1 victory over Türkiye, as Hans Niemann and Levon Aronian scored wins on the bottom two boards.

Aronian finished the event strongly, winning his final two games and collecting individual bronze on board four with 6/8.

Azerbaijan and Armeania also ended the event with match victories, defeating Serbia 2½–1½, and Croatia 3–1, respectively.

Armenia's Shant Sargsyan took individual bronze on board three, with 8/11 and a 2745 TPR | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

Hungary's seventh-place finish, one position above their seeding, was built in large part on the form of reserve player Gleb Dudin.

Dudin played ten of the eleven rounds and scored 8/10, impressively closing the Olympiad with five consecutive victories. His final win over Gukesh was the most significant of the sequence and secured him individual gold on board five with a 2738 performance rating. For a player rated, defeating the reigning world champion was an appropriate conclusion to one of the strongest individual performances of the event.

21-year-old Gleb Dudin receiving individual gold for his performance on board five alongside India's Savitha Shri | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

Erdogmus, Van Foreest and Samunenkov impress

As it is the case in every edition of the Olympiad, players away from the medal-winning teams also produced notable individual results.

Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus, aged 15, scored 8/10 for Türkiye with a 2839 TPR, earning individual silver on board one behind Abdusattorov. He gained 15.1 rating points in Samarkand and climbed to 17 th place in the live rankings, making him the highest-rated under-20 player in the world, ahead of Gukesh .

Jorden van Foreest also had an outstanding event for the Netherlands, scoring 8/10 with a 2798 TPR on board two. His tournament ended abruptly, however, when a one-move blunder against Bluebaum turned a drawn position into a final-round defeat. Van Foreest still took individual silver on board two. He finished with the same TPR as China's Wei Yi, but Wei played one additional game and took gold.

Another notable individual gold went to 17-year-old Ihor Samunenkov of Ukraine. His final-round draw against Yakubboev left him on 8/10 and gave him first place on board four, surpassing Gukesh at the last hurdle.

Jorden van Foreest and Armenia's Mariam Mkrtchyan | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

Two well-known rising starts in the chess circuit Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus and Carissa Yip | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

Ukrainian ace Ihor Samunenkov edged Gukesh Dommaraju to claim individual gold on board four | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

title: Inaugural FIDE Excellence Awards celebrate the people and achievements shaping chess worldwide
summary:
By Angelika Valkova for FIDE / Photos by KNZO Photography

The inaugural FIDE Excellence Awards were presented in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, bringing together the global chess community to celebrate outstanding achievements both on and off the board during the 2024–2026 Olympiad cycle.

Held alongside the 46 th FIDE Chess Olympiad, the ceremony honoured leading players, teams, tournaments, federations, creators and initiatives whose work has contributed to the development and global reach of chess.

Established in 2026 as a biennial programme, the FIDE Excellence Awards cover achievements from September 2024 to August 2026. Following an open nomination process, ten nominees in each of the 11 categories were shortlisted by the FIDE Excellence Awards Jury before the final recipients were determined by the FIDE Excellence Awards Panel.

The evening began with welcoming remarks from Odil Abdurakhmanov, representative of the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan for Sports, who highlighted Uzbekistan's role as a crossroads of cultures and civilizations and spoke about chess as something that reaches far beyond sporting competition – a universal language capable of bringing people together.

Viswanathan Anand then welcomed the guests and thanked the Government of Uzbekistan for its hospitality and for hosting the event in Samarkand.

Reflecting on the purpose of the awards, Anand stressed that the success of chess is built not only by its champions, but by a much wider community.

"Behind every great player, there are people who supported them, directly or indirectly: federations, coaches, arbiters, organizers, sponsors, promoters, photographers, professionals from many backgrounds who use chess as a tool to help people grow and become better", Anand said.

"Tonight is about recognising them and their efforts. The Excellence Awards are an opportunity to bring some of those achievements into the spotlight and simply say thank you. Thank you for being there when it mattered, thank you for providing support when it was important, and for seeing an opportunity that others did not", he added.

Anand concluded by congratulating all nominees and recipients and extending FIDE's gratitude to everyone contributing to the game, whether recognised during the ceremony or not.

Excellence on and around the board

The awards programme in Samarkand celebrated achievements across different areas of the chess world, from emerging talent and remarkable sporting returns to team success, inclusion, content creation, tournaments and social initiatives.

Yağız Kaan Erdoğmuş was named Best Breakthrough (Rookie of the Year), recognising the extraordinary rise of one of the world's leading young talents.

Levon Aronian received the Best Comeback award, following another remarkable chapter in his long career at the highest level.

The Best Team award went to India's Open and Women's National Teams, recognising an exceptional period for Indian chess, highlighted by the historic double gold at the 2024 Chess Olympiad in Budapest and a series of major international successes.

Łukasz Nowak was named Best Chess Player with a Disability, with Łukasz Turlej accepting the award on his behalf.

Remembering Daniel Naroditsky

A particularly meaningful moment of the evening came with the presentation of the Daniel Naroditsky Best Creator Award.

The category carries the name of the late American grandmaster, educator, commentator and content creator Daniel Naroditsky, honouring his exceptional ability to share chess knowledge and bring the game closer to audiences around the world.

Before announcing the recipient, Arkady Dvorkovich paid tribute to Naroditsky and his contribution to the chess community.

"He made an amazing contribution to promoting chess to younger generations and to everyone who loved the spirit of chess. He worked endlessly, and he was the kind of person who was loved by everyone".

Dvorkovich described preserving Naroditsky's legacy as something carrying both institutional and personal significance before announcing ChessBase India as the first recipient of the Daniel Naroditsky Best Creator Award.

As part of the recognition, the winner also receives a free spot at the next Naroditsky Memorial in Charlotte, further connecting the award with the tournament established to celebrate Naroditsky's life and legacy.

Excellence beyond the board

The ceremony continued by recognising tournaments, organisations and initiatives whose impact extends across the international chess community.

The Qatar Masters Open received first place in the Best Tournament (Open) category, followed by the Grenke Freestyle Chess Open in second place and the Sharjah Masters in third.

In the Best Tournament (Round Robin) category, Norway Chess took first place, with the Sinquefield Cup second and the Cairns Cup third. Among the developments recognised at Norway Chess was the establishment of its women's tournament with an equal prize fund.

In the Best Federation category, the Uzbekistan Chess Federation received first place, with the Kazakhstan Chess Federation taking second and the All India Chess Federation third. The award recognised the work of national federations in developing chess, supporting players and strengthening the game at both grassroots and elite levels.

The awards also celebrated projects using chess to create a broader social impact. Chess in Schools and Communities received first place for Best Chess Initiative, followed by Chess for Freedom in second and The Gift of Chess in third.

Special recognition

The evening also included a special recognition for the Bundesliga, honouring one of the world's most established and prestigious national chess leagues.

The FIDE America Social Initiatives Program 2025 was also recognised for its work across the continent. Implemented through the CCA Diversity Commission, the programme supported 14 completed initiatives across 11 countries, demonstrating how chess can be used to promote inclusion and social engagement in different communities.

The Best Chess Player (Female) and Best Chess Player (Male) awards will be presented separately during the Closing Ceremony of the 46 th FIDE Chess Olympiad, completing the inaugural FIDE Excellence Awards programme.

With the final awards of the Gala presented, the inaugural FIDE Excellence Awards evening came to a close in Samarkand, celebrating the players, teams, organisers, creators, federations and initiatives whose achievements and contributions continue to shape chess around the world.

title: Samarkand R10 (open): Uzbekistan enter final round with one-point lead over India
summary:
Five teams with chances to grab gold

Uzbekistan will enter the final round of the Chess Olympiad with a one-point lead after producing one of their most convincing performances of the tournament. The hosts defeated Armenia 3½–½ on Saturday, while India kept up the pressure with a victory by the same score against Uzbekistan 2.

With one round remaining, Uzbekistan lead on 18/20 match points, India follow on 17/20, while Germany, Ukraine and Hungary all stand on 16/20. Those are the five teams that still retain a chance of finishing first in Samarkand.

The final round will bring confrontations involving the contenders. Uzbekistan will face Ukraine, giving the latter a chance to catch the leaders on match points with a match victory. India will meet Hungary, while Germany take on the Netherlands. The Dutch belong to an eight-team group on 15/20 and are no longer in contention for first place.

The decisive round will begin four hours earlier than usual, at 8.00 CEST.

Round 11 pairings

Eastern Time

...103 boards

Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Javokhir Sindarov and Nodirbek Yakubboev were all part of the team that won the 2022 Chess Olympiad in Chennai | Photo: Rafal Oleksiewicz / FIDE

Uzbekistan make short work of unbeaten Armenia

Armenia had been one of the most resilient teams in the tournament before meeting the hosts. Through nine rounds, they had lost only two individual games, and both defeats had merely cost them a single match point in draws against higher-seeded United States and Netherlands.

Uzbekistan, however, broke through much more decisively.

Javokhir Sindarov and Mukhiddin Madaminov scored relatively quick victories after their Armenian opponents went wrong tactically in double-edged middlegames. Nodirbek Abdusattorov then added a third win, although his game against Haik Martirosyan required considerably more patience, as Abdusattorov eventually converted an endgame with rooks and opposite-coloured bishops.

The final 3½–½ score was particularly notable given how difficult Armenia had been to beat throughout the event.

A remarkable team leader, on and off the board - 22-year-old Nodirbek Abdusattorov | Photo: Rafal Oleksiewicz / FIDE

Uzbekistan's success has been built on strength across all four boards. Abdusattorov, the only member of the team to have played all ten rounds, has scored 8/10 and leads all board-one players with a 2900 tournament performance rating.

Sindarov and Yakubboev are also near the top of the individual standings. Sindarov currently sits second among board-two players, behind Jorden van Foreest of the Netherlands, while Yakubboev is second on board three behind Germany's Frederik Svane.

After nine match victories in ten rounds, Uzbekistan now need one final strong result to complete their campaign on home soil.

Javokhir Sindarov and Mukhiddin Madaminov, who both won on Saturday, are also good friends and successful collaborators | Photo: Rafal Oleksiewicz / FIDE

India remain within one point

India were facing a very different type of challenge against Uzbekistan 2. On three of the four boards, the defending champions enjoyed rating advantages of more than 200 Elo points - itself an indication of how strongly Uzbekistan's second team had over-performed to reach the top tables in round ten.

The rating gap eventually showed in the result. Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, Nihal Sarin and Gukesh Dommaraju all won, while Arjun Erigaisi drew Abdimalik Abdisalimov to complete a 3½–½ victory.

Once again, Gukesh made an important contribution. The world champion has now scored 8½/10 and, like Abdusattorov, has played in every round. His 2797 tournament performance rating makes him the clear favourite for individual gold on board four.

His form has also been particularly valuable in the closing stages. In round nine, Gukesh had been the player who decided India's match against Germany, defeating Alexander Donchenko in the only decisive game of a 2½–1½ victory.

India will now finish against Hungary, knowing that anything less than a win would make it extremely difficult to overhaul Uzbekistan.

Gukesh Dommaraju is having a great run in Samarkand | Photo: Michal Walusza / FIDE

Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu remains undefeated on board one, with 6/9 points to his name | Photo: Michal Walusza / FIDE

Ukraine earn their first major upset

Ukraine kept their title chances alive with their most important result of the event so far, beating fourth-seeded China 3–1. It was Ukraine's first upset match victory of the Olympiad, and it came at exactly the right moment.

Igor Kovalenko defeated Ding Liren on board one, while 18-year-old European champion Roman Dehtiarov beat Kong Xiangrui on board four. The other two games ended drawn, with Vasyl Ivanchuk holding Wei Yi and Ihor Samunenkov sharing the point with Xu Xiangyu.

Samunenkov has been Ukraine's most consistent individual performer. The 17-year-old has scored 7½/9 on board four and currently sits second in the individual rankings on that board, behind only Gukesh.

Igor Kovalenko defeated none other than former world champion Ding Liren on the top board | Photo: Michal Walusza / FIDE

Roman Dehtiarov converting his advantage against Kong Xiangrui as captain Alexander Beliavsky follows the action closely | Photo: Michal Walusza / FIDE

Svane brothers deliver once again

Germany also remained in the race by defeating France 3–1, and the pattern of the match was by now a familiar one.

Vincent Keymer and Matthias Bluebaum drew on the top two boards, while Frederik and Rasmus Svane supplied the wins on boards three and four. The same script had already worked for Germany against Türkiye and, more importantly, against Uzbekistan earlier in the tournament. The two brothers have repeatedly provided the decisive points when Germany have needed them.

Frederik Svane, in particular, has had an outstanding event. He leads the individual standings on board three with 8/10 and a 2819 tournament performance rating.

Germany's final opponents will be the Netherlands, who defeated Romania 2½–1½ in round ten thanks to Jorden van Foreest's victory on board two.

With the Svane brothers as team heroes, Germany beat France to remain in contention for overall victory | Photo: Rafal Oleksiewicz / FIDE

Hungary stay in contention

Hungary are the fifth team still mathematically capable of taking first place after defeating Spain 3–1. Their match was quite different from Germany's, as all four games ended decisively. Richard Rapport, Peter Leko and Gleb Dudin scored the Hungarian wins, while Jaime Santos Latasa defeated Benjamin Gledura for Spain.

Dudin, who entered the tournament as Hungary's reserve, has become one of the team's most reliable scorers. He now has 7/9 and enters the final round on a run of four consecutive victories. That form could be important against India, with both teams needing a win to maximise their chances at the top.

Behind the five title contenders, eight teams stand on 15/20: the United States, Azerbaijan, Türkiye, Croatia, Uzbekistan 2, the Netherlands, Armenia and Serbia.

title: Timur Turlov elected President of FIDE
summary:
FIDE press release

Delegates representing 196 national chess federations took part in the election, with three candidates competing in the race. In the first round, Turlov received 96 votes, Wadim Rosenstein (Germany) received 76 votes, and Jan Henric Buettner (Germany) received 20 votes. In total, 192 votes were cast.

In the second round, which followed two hours later, Turlov won by a vote of 110 to 85 (196 votes in total), becoming the eighth President of FIDE. He succeeded Arkady Dvorkovich, who served two terms as President, from 2018 to 2026.

"We are all one family, and we will continue working as one. This is a great responsibility and a vote for a better future of our sport," Timur Turlov said following the result.

"I am grateful to everyone who supported my campaign and to everyone who took part in this election. We may have different opinions, but we all share one belief – that chess is important and that we can do much more to develop it around the world by making our Member Federations stronger and more independent," he added.

"I look forward to moving chess forward and giving the game the spotlight it deserves," Turlov concluded.

In his congratulations to Timur Turlov, former FIDE President Arkady Dvorkovich wished him success in his work.

"Timur has already done a great deal for chess, and I am sure he will do even more now as FIDE President. He and his team have the energy, a clear plan, and resources to deliver and this election result shows Timur has significant backing. We are all one family, and we all share the same goal – for chess to be bigger, better and stronger in the world," Dvorkovich said.

Abdulla Aripov, Prime Minister of Uzbekistan, host of both the 46th FIDE Olympiad and the FIDE Congress, greeted those attending and noted the country’s commitment to promoting chess and friendship in the world.

Biography: Timur Turlov

Timur Turlov (born on 13 November 1987) is an economist and serves as the Chief Executive Officer of Freedom Holding Corp., an international financial services group listed on the NASDAQ Stock Exchange, with a capitalisation of nearly $11 billion.

Since January 2023, he has served as President of the Kazakhstan Chess Federation. Turlov is also the founding President of the International School Chess Federation (ISCF), established in September 2024.

Playing chess since childhood, Turlov – a father of six – has supported chess tournaments in Kazakhstan and abroad. Over three years, Freedom Holding Corp. allocated approximately $30 million to the development of chess in Kazakhstan and supported the staging of more than 20 major international FIDE tournaments, becoming one of the largest private sponsors of the game worldwide.

In September 2024, together with FIDE, Turlov initiated the founding of the International School Chess Federation and serves as its President. With a strong belief in the value of education and the role of chess in personal and professional development, the ISCF works with schools, educational organisations, NGOs and national federations to expand chess in education and promote the game among young people worldwide.

He chairs the Turkic Chess Association, which brings together the national chess federations of Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, Türkiye and Uzbekistan. Under the Association’s auspices, the inaugural Turkic Countries Team Chess Championship was held in Astana in 2026.

With a deep connection to chess tradition and a strong belief in innovation, Timur Turlov advocates the use of digital solutions to help FIDE and national federations advance modern, transparent and sustainable governance, improve services and provide more effective support for players and chess communities around the world.
